messages.subject: Rhadoop read text file file
parts:
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Data Dictionary (9 columns)
- Id: Unique identifier of the article
- Article_Title: Title of the article published in HBR
- Source : Source would be single category i.e. Harvard Business Review
- Pub_Date: Publishing date of the article on HBR
- Volume: Publishing volume of HBR
- Issue: Publishing issue of HBR
- Page_Count: Length of the article in pages
- Document_Type: Type of the article published i.e. article, case study, editorial etc.
- Abstract: Abstract of the article published on HBR
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
---------------------------------------------------------------------------


---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Sample data
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 [1] "1\tOrganization.\tHarvard Business Review\t1998-01-01\t76\t1\t2\tArticle\t\"The article looks at how marketing departments can better communicate with other departments within an organization. The author suggests that the marketing department is the first and main source of knowledge about the customer but it often struggles to share its insights with the rest of the organization. Details related to research on the issue by Elliot Maltz of the University of Southern California and Ajay Kohli of the University of Texas are reviewed. Comments from Maltz are included. Issues related to the communication skills of marketing managers are discussed. The author states that content, timing and presentation are all important parts of business communication.\""                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    
  [2] "2\tJoint Ventures.\tHarvard Business Review\t1998-01-01\t76\t1\t2\tArticle\t\"The author looks at how international joint ventures are facing the challenge of delegating which tasks should be performed at their headquarters and which ones should be delegated to on-site managers. Research on the issue conducted by Yoram Zeira of Tel Aviv University and William Newburry of New York University's Stern School of Business is discussed. According to Newburry, parent companies are better off leaving the more administrative duties to the on-site managers. The study focuses on areas that fall into a gray area of responsibility between corporate parents and joint ventures, including the creation and implementation of a strategic plan, authority over human resources policy, and control over whether the venture's top management should come from the dominant parent. Differences related to the issue in developed and non-developed countries are analyzed.\""                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 
  [3] "3\tMarketing.\tHarvard Business Review\t1998-01-01\t76\t1\t3\tArticle\t\"The article discusses new research showing that companies can get more useful ideas out of focus groups by computerizing the process. According to the author, facilitators can better control the behavior of a focus group by using software specifically designed for the process. The article states that the software allows each group member to have an equal voice, helps members stay focused on the task at hand, brainstorm more effectively, and make decision faster. However, it is suggested that focus group participants do not prefer a computer aided experience. Details related to research conducted regarding the issue by Michael Parent of the University of Wester Ontario, et al. are discussed.\""                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      
  [4] "4\tInternational Business.\tHarvard Business Review\t1998-01-01\t76\t1\t3\tArticle\t\"The article looks at how few Western business are deciding to include sub-Saharan Africa in their plans for global expansion. The author reviews how poverty, lack of education, and an underdeveloped infrastructure are viewed as obstacles to achieving business success in the region. Research on companies that have found success in countries like Botswana, Cameroon, Ghana and Zimbabwe, conducted by Harvard Business School professor James E. Austin, et al., is discussed. According to the study, companies that have succeeded in sub-Saharan Africa improvised and innovated, had keen familiarity with the local business environment, which was a function of local ownership or the active involvement of managers or partners from the region, and had obtained technology, technological advice, or product licensing from outside the region.\""                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
---------------------------------------------------------------------------



---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Code for reading file
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
col.classes = 
  c(Id = "character", Article_Title = "character", Source = "character", 
    Pub_Date = "character", Volume = "character", Issue = "character",
    Page_Count = "numeric", Document_Type = "character", Abstract = "character")

inp.format =
  read.table(
    "data.txt", 
    sep = "\t",
    col.names = names(col.classes),
    colClasses = col.classes),
    fill = TRUE,
    na.strings = "NA")

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

messages.subject: Re: Rhadoop read text file file
parts: First we need to see line 123 to have an idea. It's clearly not the spaces because those are in every line apparently. Number two, I am little confused by the escaped quotes: are those escaped in the file itself or not? That's controlled by read.table option allowEscape, which you can use with make.input.format as well, for csv only.
